pos: n. (capital of Norway; episcopal see whose bishop accepted the Reformation imposed from Denmark in 1537)
etymology: From Old Norse Ósló, probably the meadow at the river mouth; óss, mouth, and ló, meadow.
biblical_def: Oslo received the Reformation rather than made it. Norway in 1537 was not a kingdom that reformed itself but a realm under the Danish crown, and the Church Ordinance was extended to it by the king who had won the civil war. Hans Rev, the bishop of Oslo, accepted the change and kept his seat as superintendent; the monasteries were dissolved, the cathedral school continued as a Latin school, and a generation passed before there were enough Norwegian-speaking evangelical preachers to fill the parishes. The dictionary records Oslo because it is the clearest northern case of a reformation that began as a political fact and became, slowly and unevenly, a spiritual one. The pattern is not therefore false. God opens hearts one at a time whatever the circumstance that brought the preacher into the room, and Luke is careful to credit the opening to the right agent: Lydia heard Paul, “whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul” (Act 16:14). An ordinance can put a preacher in a pulpit. It cannot do that.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to ordain as to appoint, to decree, to establish by law; a see as the seat of episcopal power, a diocese; and to perform as to execute, to accomplish, to carry through to completion.
webster_full: ORDAIN, v.t. [L. ordino.] To set in order; to appoint; to decree; to establish by law or edict.
SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.
PERFORM, v.t. To do; to execute; to accomplish; to carry through to completion.
SUPERINTENDENT, n. One who has the oversight and charge of something, with the power of direction.
scriptures: And a certain woman named Lydia, a seller of purple, of the city of Thyatira, which worshipped God, heard us: whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul.
Php 1:6
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ:

Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you, and ordained you, that ye should go and bring forth fruit, and that your fruit should remain: that whatsoever ye shall ask of the Father in my name, he may give it you.
A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.
corruption_summary: Norway's capital see, whose bishop accepted the Reformation extended from Denmark in 1537 and continued as superintendent.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the confidence that a right establishment will of itself produce a believing people, and its mirror image, the contempt for any reformation that came by lawful authority rather than by popular conviction. Norway suffered the first and is often judged by the second. The ordinance of 1537 gave the country evangelical forms before it had evangelical faith; what filled them was two centuries of catechising, and after that the Haugean awakening.

The principle to recover is that God finishes what He begins and that the work is His from first to last. Paul is confident of a congregation on no other ground, “that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Php 1:6). Christ puts the initiative beyond dispute, “Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you” (Joh 15:16). And the promise of the new covenant is of a changed nature, not a changed polity: “A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you” (Eze 36:26).
roots_summary: Greek dianoigo (G1272), to open thoroughly; Hebrew leb (H3820), the heart.
roots_lines: Greek dianoigo (G1272) — to open up completely, to open the understanding; Acts 16:14.
Hebrew leb (H3820) — the heart, the inner man, the will; Ezekiel 36:26.
Greek epiteleo (G2005) — to complete, to perform, to bring to an end; Philippians 1:6.
Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out, to select for oneself; John 15:16.
Hebrew ruach (H7307) — wind, breath, spirit; Ezekiel 36:26.
usage: “whose heart the Lord opened, that she attended unto the things which were spoken of Paul” (Act 16:14) — the ordinance of 1537 extended to Norway.
“that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Php 1:6) — Bishop Hans Rev continues as superintendent.
“A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you” (Eze 36:26) — a generation before there were Norwegian preachers enough.

pos: n. (inland Norwegian town; medieval bishopric suppressed at the Reformation and merged into the see of Oslo)
etymology: From Old Norse hamarr, a rocky outcrop or crag.
biblical_def: Hamar was one of the five medieval Norwegian bishoprics and the only one to be abolished. Founded in 1152 beside Lake Mjosa, it governed the inland valleys; its last bishop, Mogens Lauritssøn, refused the Reformation, was besieged in his fortified residence in 1537 and carried off to imprisonment in Denmark, where he died. The see was not given an evangelical superintendent but simply dissolved and its territory joined to Oslo; the cathedral fell into ruin and stands today as a shell under glass. The dictionary records Hamar because a bishopric can be taken away, and the removal of a church is a judgment Scripture describes rather than a mere accident of politics. Christ warns a real congregation in these terms, telling Ephesus to remember whence it is fallen and repent, “or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place” (Rev 2:5). The warning assumes what Hamar demonstrates: that an ancient and well-endowed see has no guarantee of continuance.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a candlestick as an instrument or utensil to hold a candle; a diocese as the circuit or extent of a bishop's jurisdiction; and to remove as to cause to change place, to put from its place.
webster_full: CANDLESTICK, n. An instrument or utensil to hold a candle, made in different forms and of different materials.
DIOCESE, n. [Gr.] The circuit or extent of a bishop's jurisdiction; an ecclesiastical division of a kingdom or state.
REMOVE, v.t. To cause to change place; to put from its place in any manner; to displace.
RUIN, n. [L. ruina.] Destruction; fall; overthrow; defeat; also, the remains of a decayed or demolished building.
scriptures: Rev 2:5
Remember therefore from whence thou art fallen, and repent, and do the first works; or else I will come unto thee quickly, and will remove thy candlestick out of his place, except thou repent.
Rev 1:20

The mystery of the seven stars which thou sawest in my right hand, and the seven golden candlesticks. The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches: and the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches.
Therefore say I unto you, The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof.
For if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee.
corruption_summary: The only Norwegian bishopric abolished rather than reformed; its last bishop died a prisoner in Denmark and its cathedral is a ruin.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the doctrine of indefectibility as applied to institutions: the assumption that a church which has stood for four centuries will stand for a fifth, and that antiquity is itself a warrant. Rome applies this to a see; Protestants apply it to denominations, colleges and congregations with the same false confidence. Hamar had four hundred years of standing and a cathedral to prove it, and it has neither bishop nor roof.

The principle to recover is that the lampstands are held in Christ's hand and may be taken out of it. John is given the key himself, that “the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches” (Rev 1:20). Christ had said the same of a whole people, that “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you, and given to a nation bringing forth the fruits thereof” (Mat 21:43). Paul presses the lesson on Gentile presumption in one line: “For if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee” (Rom 11:21).
roots_summary: Greek luchnia (G3087), a candlestick; Greek metanoeo (G3340), to repent.
roots_lines: Greek luchnia (G3087) — a lampstand, a candlestick; Revelation 1:20.
Greek metanoeo (G3340) — to change the mind, to repent; Revelation 2:5.
Greek kineo (G2795) — to move, to remove out of place; Revelation 2:5.
Greek airo (G142) — to lift, to take away; Matthew 21:43.
Greek kladoi (G2798) — branches, boughs; Romans 11:21.

“the seven candlesticks which thou sawest are the seven churches” (Rev 1:20) — its last bishop died a prisoner in Denmark.
“For if God spared not the natural branches, take heed lest he also spare not thee” (Rom 11:21) — the cathedral a shell under glass.

pos: n. (the medieval archiepiscopal see of Norway, the city now called Trondheim; shrine of Olaf and the northern pilgrimage centre)
etymology: From Old Norse Niðaróss, the mouth of the river Nid; renamed Trondheim in later use.
biblical_def: Nidaros was the religious capital of the North Atlantic world. Made an archbishopric in 1152, it held jurisdiction over Norway, Iceland, Greenland, the Faroes, Orkney, Shetland and the Isle of Man, and its cathedral housed the shrine of King Olaf, killed in 1030 and venerated as a saint, to which pilgrims came from all Scandinavia and beyond. The last archbishop, Olav Engelbrektsson, led the resistance to the Reformation, fought for the Catholic claimant in the civil war, and in 1537 fled to the Netherlands with the cathedral treasure, dying in exile the next year. The shrine was stripped and the saint's body removed. The dictionary records Nidaros under its ecclesiastical name because the pilgrimage is the point: a nation taught for four centuries to seek access to God through a dead king. Scripture leaves exactly one channel open, and names Him: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5). Every shrine in Christendom is a denial of that verse in architecture.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mediator as one who interposes between parties at variance, and in theology Christ, who is the mediator between God and man; a shrine as a case in which sacred things are deposited; and a pilgrimage as a journey to some place deemed sacred.
webster_full: MEDIATOR, n. [L. mediator.] One that interposes between parties at variance for the purpose of reconciling them; by way of eminence, Christ is the mediator between God and man.
SHRINE, n. [L. scrinium.] A case, box or receptacle for holding sacred things; a place or object hallowed from its history or associations.
PILGRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable, in order to pay devotion to the relics of some deceased saint.
RELIC, n. [L. reliquiae.] That which remains; the remains of the body of a saint, to which the Romanists attribute efficacy.
scriptures: For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
Joh 14:6
Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.
Act 4:12
Neither is there salvation in any other: for there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved.
Heb 7:25
Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
corruption_summary: The archiepiscopal see of the North Atlantic and the shrine of Olaf; its last archbishop fled in 1537 with the treasure.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption is Roman and it is not historical only. The cult of the saints offers the believer intercessors who are nearer, kinder or more approachable than Christ, and in doing so it slanders Him; the shrine makes the offer physical, and the pilgrimage makes it expensive. Modern Rome has not withdrawn the doctrine, and the pilgrim route to Nidaros has been revived in our own day as heritage and spirituality, which keeps the practice while mislaying even the old reason for it.

The principle to recover is that access to the Father is single, direct and permanently open. Christ allows no alternative: “I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6). Peter denies that any other name exists for the purpose, for “there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12). And Hebrews grounds the sufficiency in His endless life, that He “is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him” (Heb 7:25), since He ever lives to make intercession.
roots_summary: Greek mesites (G3316), a mediator; Greek entugchano (G1793), to intercede.
roots_lines: Greek mesites (G3316) — a go-between, a mediator, an arbitrator; 1 Timothy 2:5.
Greek entugchano (G1793) — to plead for, to make intercession; Hebrews 7:25.
Greek hodos (G3598) — a way, a road, a route; John 14:6.
Greek panteles (G3838) — complete, to the uttermost, perfectly; Hebrews 7:25.
Greek onoma (G3686) — a name, and by implication authority; Acts 4:12.
usage: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus” (1Ti 2:5) — the shrine of Olaf stripped in 1537.
“I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me” (Joh 14:6) — four centuries of pilgrimage ended.
“there is none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved” (Act 4:12) — Archbishop Engelbrektsson dead in exile, 1538.

pos: n. (chief city and port of western Norway; Hanseatic trading station and evangelical see from 1537)
etymology: From Old Norse Björgvin, the meadow among the mountains; berg, mountain.
biblical_def: Bergen was the largest city in Norway and the least Norwegian. The German merchants of the Hanseatic League held the wharf called Bryggen as a walled compound with their own law, their own clergy and their own language, and they had brought Lutheran preaching into the city before the Danish crown reformed the realm. Geble Pedersson, the first evangelical bishop of Norway, held the see from 1537 and gathered a circle of humanist scholars around him; his nephew Absalon Pederssøn Beyer taught in the cathedral school. The reformation of Bergen therefore came partly through resident foreigners whose motives were mixed and whose commercial privileges the Norwegians resented. The dictionary records the city because the word of God travels on trade routes and in the mouths of strangers, and the church is not permitted to despise the carrier. Peter had to learn this in a Gentile house and said so plainly: “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons” (Act 10:34).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a stranger as a foreigner, one who belongs to another country; a merchant as one who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries; and a respecter of persons as one who regards the outward condition of men.
webster_full: STRANGER, n. [L. extraneus.] A foreigner; one who belongs to another country; one unknown.
MERCHANT, n. [L. mercor, to buy.] A man who trafficks or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who exports and imports goods and sells them by wholesale.
RESPECT, n. [L. respectus.] Regard; attention; partial regard; undue bias to the prejudice of justice.
WHARF, n. A perpendicular bank or mound of timber or stone, raised on the shore of a harbor for the convenience of lading and unlading ships.
scriptures: Then Peter opened his mouth, and said, Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons:
But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him.
Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt.
But the stranger that dwelleth with you shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt: I am the LORD your God.
corruption_summary: Norway's chief port, where Hanseatic Germans brought Lutheran preaching before the crown did; Geble Pedersson's see from 1537.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the judging of a message by the standing of its messenger. The Bergen Norwegians had real grievances against the German wharf, and it would have been easy to refuse the doctrine along with the privileges. The reverse error is equally live, the flattery of the foreign and fashionable simply because it comes from elsewhere. Scripture forbids both by forbidding respect of persons altogether.

The principle to recover is that God accepts men without regard to nation, and that His people must deal with the resident foreigner as with one of their own. Peter completes his sentence thus: “But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him” (Act 10:35). The law had long since required the affection and given the reason, “Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Deu 10:19), and it fixed the standard of treatment at the highest point available: the stranger “shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself” (Lev 19:34).
roots_summary: Greek prosopoleptes (G4381), a respecter of persons; Hebrew ger (H1616), a sojourner.
roots_lines: Greek prosopoleptes (G4381) — one who shews partiality, a respecter of persons; Acts 10:34.
Hebrew ger (H1616) — a sojourner, a resident alien, a stranger; Leviticus 19:34.
Greek dektos (G1184) — acceptable, accepted; Acts 10:35.
Hebrew ahab (H157) — to love; Deuteronomy 10:19.
Greek ethnos (G1484) — a nation, a people; Acts 10:35.
usage: “Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons” (Act 10:34) — Lutheran preaching on the German wharf before 1537.
“Love ye therefore the stranger: for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Deu 10:19) — Geble Pedersson, first evangelical bishop of Norway.
“shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself” (Lev 19:34) — a humanist circle in the cathedral school.

pos: n. (town and see of south-west Norway; the smallest medieval Norwegian bishopric, reformed in 1537)
etymology: From Old Norse Stafangr, probably the staff-shaped inlet; stafr, staff, and angr, bay.
biblical_def: Stavanger held the smallest and poorest of the Norwegian bishoprics, founded about 1125 and governing the south-western coast from a cathedral that still stands. Its last Roman bishop, Hoskuld Hoskuldsson, died in 1537 as the Reformation arrived, and the see passed to evangelical superintendents; it was moved inland to Kristiansand in 1682 and not restored to Stavanger until 1925. The town remained a fishing and timber port of a few thousand people, and in the nineteenth century it became the heart of the Haugean lay revival and the cradle of Norwegian foreign missions, sending men out in numbers wholly disproportionate to its size. The dictionary records Stavanger because the smallness is the lesson. Zechariah rebukes the men who weighed the second temple against the first and found it contemptible, asking: “For who hath despised the day of small things?” (Zec 4:10). The eyes of the LORD run through the whole earth, and they are not looking for large congregations.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines small as slender, minute, of little moment; a grain as a single seed of corn; and to confound as to perplex, to abash, to put to shame and silence.
webster_full: SMALL, adj. Slender; minute; fine; of little size; of little moment, weight or importance.
GRAIN, n. [L. granum.] Any small hard mass; a single seed or kernel of corn, or any similar fruit.
CONFOUND, v.t. [L. confundo.] To perplex; to abash; to throw the mind into disorder; to put to shame and silence.
MUSTARD, n. A plant of the genus Sinapis, the seeds of which are of a hot pungent taste.
scriptures: Zec 4:10

For who hath despised the day of small things? for they shall rejoice, and shall see the plummet in the hand of Zerubbabel with those seven; they are the eyes of the LORD, which run to and fro through the whole earth.
Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field:
Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs, and becometh a tree, so that the birds of the air come and lodge in the branches thereof.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
corruption_summary: The smallest and poorest Norwegian see, and later the heart of the Haugean revival and the cradle of Norwegian missions.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the measuring of a church by its scale, which produces contempt for the small congregation and anxiety in it. Where size is the test, a faithful country parish is a failure and a crowded one is beyond criticism, and both judgments are false. Stavanger was negligible by every measure the age used and it sent missionaries across the world.

The principle to recover is that God works through what looks insufficient, and that He chooses it deliberately so the glory cannot be mistaken. Christ compares His kingdom to a seed and names its insignificance first: it is “like to a grain of mustard seed, which a man took, and sowed in his field” (Mat 13:31), and “Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs” (Mat 13:32). Paul states the principle as a settled policy of God, who “hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27).

roots_lines: Hebrew qaton (H6996) — small, little, of no account; Zechariah 4:10.
Greek kokkos (G2848) — a kernel, a grain, a seed; Matthew 13:31.

Greek kataischuno (G2617) — to put to shame, to confound; 1 Corinthians 1:27.

“Which indeed is the least of all seeds: but when it is grown, it is the greatest among herbs” (Mat 13:32) — the heart of the Haugean revival.

pos: n. (first evangelical superintendent of Nidaros, died 1548; a Norwegian trained at Wittenberg and sent home to reform his own country)
etymology: From Old Norse Thorbjörn, the bear of Thor; Bratt, a byname meaning steep or abrupt.
biblical_def: Torbjorn Olavsson Bratt was the first Norwegian to reform Norwegians. Born in Nidaros, he went to Wittenberg, took his degree there, heard Luther and Melanchthon, and was recommended by Luther himself when the archbishopric he had grown up under fell vacant by the archbishop's flight. He returned in 1546 as superintendent of the see, preached in Norwegian in the cathedral where the shrine of Olaf had stood, set up a Latin school, and had barely two years in the office before he died in 1548. His few sermons that survive are the earliest evangelical preaching in Norwegian that we possess. The dictionary records him because the Reformation in Norway is usually told as a Danish imposition, and he is the standing exception: a native, speaking the language, sent back to his own town. Christ sent the Gerasene the same way, refusing to take him along and giving him a nearer errand instead: “Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee” (Mar 5:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a witness as one who gives testimony; an ambassador as a minister of the highest rank sent to a foreign court; and to declare as to make known, to tell explicitly.
webster_full: WITNESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; also, one who gives testimony or evidence.
AMBASSADOR, n. A minister of the highest rank employed by one prince or state at the court of another, to manage the public concerns of his own prince or state.
DECLARE, v.t. [L. declaro.] To clear; to free from obscurity; to make plain; to make known; to tell explicitly.
REDEEM, v.t. [L. redimo.] To purchase back; to ransom; to liberate or rescue from captivity or bondage by paying a price.
scriptures: Mar 5:19
Howbeit Jesus suffered him not, but saith unto him, Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee.
Let the redeemed of the LORD say so, whom he hath redeemed from the hand of the enemy;
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us: we pray you in Christ's stead, be ye reconciled to God.
corruption_summary: The Wittenberg-trained Norwegian who came home in 1546 as superintendent of Nidaros and died two years later.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error nearer at hand is the belief that a mission must be carried by foreigners to be a mission at all, with the corollary that a man sent to his own people has taken an easier road. Bratt had the harder road. He preached against the shrine his own city had lived on, to neighbours who remembered him as a boy, and it cost him what remained of his health.

The principle to recover is that the ordinary direction of testimony is outward from where the man already stands. Christ fixes the order Himself, from Jerusalem to Judaea to Samaria and then “unto the uttermost part of the earth” (Act 1:8), with home first and not last. The psalmist lays the duty on the ransomed as such: “Let the redeemed of the LORD say so” (Psa 107:2). And Paul describes the office in terms that make the humblest preacher a representative of the court he comes from, “Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us” (2Co 5:20).

roots_lines: Greek martus (G3144) — a witness, one who testifies; Acts 1:8.
Greek presbeuo (G4243) — to be an ambassador, to act as an envoy; 2 Corinthians 5:20.

Hebrew gaal (H1350) — to redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer; Psalm 107:2.

“Let the redeemed of the LORD say so” (Psa 107:2) — the earliest surviving evangelical sermons in Norwegian.
“Now then we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God did beseech you by us” (2Co 5:20) — two years in the office, dead in 1548.

pos: n. (bishop of Bergen, 1510–1582; removed the images and side altars from Bergen cathedral in 1570 against the merchants' protest)
etymology: From Danish Skjelderup, a place name; the given name Jens a northern form of John.
biblical_def: Jens Skjelderup was a physician before he was a bishop, and he applied a surgeon's decision to the furniture of his cathedral. Appointed to Bergen in 1557, he found the church still full of medieval images, carved altars and the shrines the German merchants had endowed and continued to honour, and in 1570 he had them taken out. The German wharf complained loudly, sued, and appealed to Copenhagen; the king upheld the bishop. Skjelderup defended the act in writing on the ground of the second commandment and held the see until his death in 1582. The dictionary records him because the removal of images is the point at which Reformed conviction becomes visible and expensive, and because the usual objection, that the images were only reminders, was made to him and answered. The commandment does not distinguish between an image worshipped and an image merely kept for devotion: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4). The making is forbidden before the bowing is mentioned.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an image as a representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; graven as carved or engraved; and jealous as suspicious, and in Scripture emulous, requiring exclusive devotion.
webster_full: IMAGE, n. [L. imago.] A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; a statue; a picture; an idol.
GRAVEN, participle passive. Carved; engraved; cut, as letters or figures, on a hard substance.
JEALOUS, adj. Suspicious that we do not enjoy the affection or respect of others; in Scripture, requiring exclusive devotion.
ALTAR, n. [L. altare.] A mount; an elevation of earth, stone or other material, on which sacrifices were offered.
scriptures: Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
Exo 20:5

Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;
Isa 42:8
I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
corruption_summary: Physician turned bishop of Bergen, who stripped the cathedral of its images in 1570 and was sued by the German merchants for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The live corruption is the defence of religious imagery as pedagogy, the claim that a statue teaches the unlettered and is therefore permitted. Rome has made this argument since Gregory the Great and makes it still; the Eastern churches make a stronger version of it for icons and venerate them openly. The dictionary rejects both. Where images of God or of the saints stand in a place of worship, devotion attaches itself to them whatever the official distinction says, as the Bergen merchants' lawsuit demonstrated by the vehemence of their attachment.

The principle to recover is the second commandment entire, including its reason. God forbids the bowing as well as the making, “Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them” (Exo 20:5), and grounds the prohibition in His own jealousy. He will not share His glory with an artefact: “my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images” (Isa 42:8). The psalmist reduces every such object to its materials and its maker, for “Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands” (Psa 115:4). Deuteronomy commanded Israel to deal with them physically, that “ye shall destroy their altars, and break down their images” (Deu 7:5), and Hezekiah is commended because “He removed the high places, and brake the images” (2Ki 18:4).

pos: n. (Norwegian preacher, historian and diarist, 1528–1575; author of On the Kingdom of Norway and of the Bergen Diary)
etymology: From Hebrew Abshalom (H53), father of peace; the patronymic Pederssøn, son of Peder.
biblical_def: Absalon Pederssonn, commonly called Beyer, was the nephew and heir of Geble Pedersson, bishop of Bergen, and the most articulate Norwegian of the Reformation generation. He taught in the cathedral school, lectured and preached in the city, and wrote two works that survive: Om Norgis Rige, On the Kingdom of Norway, finished in 1567, which laments the decay of a kingdom once great and now a Danish province; and a diary of Bergen life kept for sixteen years, which is the best record of a Norwegian town in that century. He also helped burn the last of the cathedral's images. The dictionary records him because lament over a nation's decline is a biblical act when it is done the biblical way: honestly, without flattering the past, and ending in repentance rather than in grievance. Jeremiah's Lamentations begin with exactly Absalon's subject and exactly his tone: “How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people!” (Lam 1:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to lament as to mourn, to bewail, to express sorrow; a chronicle as a historical account of facts in the order of time; and glory as praise, honour, splendour, brightness.
webster_full: LAMENT, v.i. [L. lamentor.] To mourn; to weep or wail; to express sorrow; to bewail.
CHRONICLE, n. [Gr. time.] An historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; a register.
GLORY, n. [L. gloria.] Praise ascribed in adoration; honor; splendor; brightness; magnificence.
SOLITARY, adj. [L. solitarius.] Living alone; retired; remote from society; also, lonely, destitute of company.
scriptures: Lam 1:1
How doth the city sit solitary, that was full of people! how is she become as a widow! she that was great among the nations, and princess among the provinces, how is she become tributary!
Hag 2:3
Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory? and how do ye see it now? is it not in your eyes in comparison of it as nothing?
Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
For thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof.
corruption_summary: Bergen humanist and preacher; his 1567 lament for Norway and his sixteen-year town diary are the best Norwegian records of the age.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is nostalgia used as a substitute for repentance. A people that mourns its lost greatness while refusing to name the sins that lost it has only exchanged one vanity for another, and the lament becomes a grievance against neighbours, foreigners or the age. Absalon is not wholly clear of this; his book blames the Danes freely. But he also blames his countrymen, and that is what makes it a lament rather than a complaint.

The principle to recover is that the right response to decline is to ask for the old ways and then walk in them. Haggai put the comparison to the men who wept over the second temple, asking “Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory? and how do ye see it now?” (Hag 2:3), and then told them to build. Jeremiah gives the method and records the refusal in one verse: “Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16). And the psalmist marks the sign of a coming mercy, that “thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof” (Psa 102:14).

pos: n. (Norwegian lay revivalist, 1771–1824; preached across Norway, imprisoned ten years under the Conventicle Act)
etymology: From Norwegian Hauge, a mound or hill, the name of his father's farm.
biblical_def: Hans Nielsen Hauge was a farmer's son from Tune who, at the age of twenty-five in 1796, became convinced that he was bound to tell his countrymen what he had come to know, and spent the next eight years walking Norway from the Swedish border to Troms, preaching in farmhouses, writing tracts that sold in tens of thousands, and setting up mills, printing works, fisheries and a shipping trade so that his followers could support themselves. The Conventicle Act of 1741 forbade lay preaching and religious meetings without a clergyman present; Hauge was arrested ten times, spent most of 1804 to 1814 in custody, and came out broken in health. The movement he left behind, the Haugeans, reshaped Norwegian Christianity for a century and went with the emigrants to Minnesota and the Dakotas. The dictionary records him because he is the clearest modern case of the office Peter gives to the whole church: “But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people” (1Pe 2:9). A man under that commission does not need a licence to say what he knows.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a priesthood as the office or character of a priest, and the order of men set apart for sacred offices; peculiar as appropriate, belonging to a person and to no other; and boldness as courage, confidence, freedom from timidity.
webster_full: PRIESTHOOD, n. The office or character of a priest; also, the order of men set apart for sacred offices.
PECULIAR, adj. [L. peculiaris.] Appropriate; belonging to a person and not to others; particular; special.
BOLDNESS, n. Courage; bravery; intrepidity; spirit; confidence; freedom from timidity.
UNLEARNED, adj. Ignorant; not learned; not versed in science and literature; illiterate.
scriptures: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Act 4:13
Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.
Amo 7:14
Then answered Amos, and said to Amaziah, I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit:
corruption_summary: The farmer's son who preached across Norway and spent most of ten years in prison for it; the Haugean movement is his monument.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is clericalism, which reserves the speaking of the gospel to a licensed order and treats the believing layman as a hearer only. Norway had it in statute law, and the statute was enforced against a sober, industrious, orthodox man for ten years. The opposite error is as real and the dictionary does not sanction it: the priesthood of all believers is not a warrant for every man to assume the pastoral office, nor for a congregation to do without ordained elders who are apt to teach.

The principle to recover is that the scattered church preaches as it goes, and that God has repeatedly used men with no standing to do it. Luke records the spread of the gospel by refugees rather than by ministers: “Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4). The council noticed the same incongruity in the apostles, when they “perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled” (Act 4:13), and took knowledge that they had been with Jesus. Amos had already disclaimed every qualification but the call: “I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman” (Amo 7:14).

pos: n. (Norwegian parish minister, historian and topographer, 1545–1614; translator of the Heimskringla and describer of Norway)
etymology: From Norwegian Claussøn, son of Claus; Friis, a family name meaning the Frisian.
biblical_def: Peder Claussonn Friis was the parish minister of Undal in southern Norway for fifty-two years and in his spare time the founder of Norwegian historical scholarship. He translated Snorri Sturluson's Heimskringla, the saga history of the Norwegian kings, out of Old Norse into Danish, which saved it for a nation that could no longer read its own medieval language; he wrote a description of Norway, its districts, rivers, fish, birds and farms, and a shorter account of Iceland and Greenland; and he did the whole of it while catechising a scattered coastal parish. The dictionary records him because the recovery and honest keeping of a nation's past is a duty Scripture repeatedly lays on the godly, and because it is usually done, as here, by a working minister rather than by an institution. The psalmist states the obligation as a refusal: “We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4). A people that cannot read its own records will be told its history by whoever profits from the telling.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chronicle as a historical account of facts in the order of time; to enquire as to ask a question, to seek information by asking; and a landmark as a mark to designate the boundary of land.
webster_full: CHRONICLE, n. [Gr. time.] An historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time; a register.
ENQUIRE, v.i. [L. inquiro.] To ask a question; to seek for truth or information by asking questions.
LANDMARK, n. A mark to designate the boundary of land; any mark or fixed object by which the limits of a farm or estate may be known.
TOPOGRAPHY, n. [Gr.] The description of a particular place, city, town, manor or tract of land.
scriptures: Job 8:8
For enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers:
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set.
corruption_summary: Parish minister of Undal for fifty-two years, who translated the Heimskringla and described Norway district by district.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the handling of history as a resource to be shaped for present use, whether by flattering a nation or by indicting it. Both methods treat the record as raw material rather than as testimony, and both are in good health. Friis did the unglamorous alternative: he translated what the sources actually said, including what was unflattering to Norway, and described what he could see with his own eyes.

The principle to recover is that the past is to be sought out, kept, and handed on without alteration. Job's friend gives the method, mistaken in his application of it but right in the counsel itself: “For enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers” (Job 8:8). The psalmist makes the transmission a succession of generations, each owing the next an account: “One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts” (Psa 145:4). And Proverbs forbids the quiet adjustment of inherited boundaries, “Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set” (Pro 22:28), which applies to a record as truly as to a field.
